description: The organization is an innovative startup in its early stages of development, currently comprised of a three-person, interdisciplinary team. It specializes in space architecture design, combining spatial design, engineering, habitation technologies, and the analysis of the needs of future users of extraterrestrial environments. The startup’s mission is to create functional and sustainable infrastructure concepts that support human presence in space.
summary:
MAREK is an interactive, multi-layer mapping and navigation support system designed for future human missions to Mars. It integrates real NASA data from orbital observations and rover missions, including Curiosity, Spirit, and Perseverance, into a unified platform featuring a global 3D map and detailed 2D exploration views.
The system enables users to analyze terrain elevation, surface temperatures, geological characteristics, and ground conditions while visualizing historical rover routes, sample locations, and proposed astronaut exploration paths.
Originally developed to identify potential sources of Martian regolith and sulfur-based materials for infrastructure construction, the project supports the concept of In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU), reducing dependence on supplies transported from Earth.
By combining geological analysis with exploration planning, MAREK helps identify potential hazards, improve route planning, and reduce astronauts' exposure to dangerous environmental conditions.
Future development will focus on real-time astronaut positioning and integration with helmet-mounted and rover-based HUD systems.
Our goal is to make Martian exploration safer, more efficient, and more sustainable while supporting the development of future human settlements.
details:
MAREK - Mars Astronaut Resource & Exploration Kit

1. Project Overview

MAREK is an interactive, multi-layer geospatial platform designed to support future human exploration of Mars. By integrating NASA's orbital observations and rover mission data into a unified environment, the system enables terrain analysis, exploration planning, and the identification of areas with potential resources for Martian infrastructure development.

The project addresses one of the fundamental challenges of establishing a sustainable human presence on Mars: how to explore an unfamiliar and potentially hazardous environment while efficiently identifying and utilizing locally available resources. Our solution follows the principles of In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU), which aims to reduce dependence on Earth-based supplies by using materials available directly on Mars.

Initially, the project focused on identifying regions containing Martian regolith and sulfur-bearing materials that could potentially be used to produce construction materials, including sulfur-based concrete and other regolith-derived composites.

Such materials could eventually contribute to the construction of roads, landing infrastructure, protective structures, and shielding for future Martian habitats. By combining geospatial visualization, geological analysis, and exploration planning, MAREK transforms scientific datasets into practical information that could support future astronaut operations.

2. Scientific Data and System Architecture

MAREK integrates datasets obtained from NASA's robotic exploration missions and orbital observation instruments.

The platform incorporates information from the Curiosity, Spirit, and Perseverance missions, alongside orbital datasets describing the physical and geological characteristics of the Martian surface.

The global mapping layers are based on data from several NASA instruments:

  • Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA): Provides topographic elevation data used to analyze terrain morphology and identify significant changes in surface elevation.
  • Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM): Provides spectral observations supporting the identification and analysis of mineralogical characteristics.
  • Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS): Supplies thermal observations and mineralogical information relevant to understanding surface conditions.

At the local exploration level, the platform incorporates geochemical information obtained from instruments such as:

  • ChemCam: Provides elemental composition measurements from the Curiosity rover.
  • SuperCam: Provides spectroscopic observations and compositional information from the Perseverance rover.

By combining orbital-scale observations with localized rover measurements, the system provides complementary perspectives on Martian terrain and potential resource distribution. This approach allows users to examine broad geological patterns while accessing more detailed information from previously explored regions.

3. Interactive Mapping and Visualization

The platform features a two-level visualization architecture designed to support both global exploration planning and detailed analysis of specific mission areas.

Level 1 – Global Mars Visualization (3D)

The global interface provides an interactive three-dimensional representation of Mars, highlighting selected NASA exploration missions. Users can switch between five thematic layers:

Basic – Surface Visualization. Displays the Martian surface and provides a general geographic overview of the planet.

Elevation – Terrain and Topography. Visualizes terrain elevation and surface morphology, supporting the identification of slopes, elevation changes, and potentially challenging terrain.

Thermal – Surface Temperature Distribution. Presents surface temperature information, enabling preliminary assessments of thermal conditions across different Martian regions.

Geology – Geological and Mineralogical Characteristics. Displays geological information and helps identify regions with potentially valuable mineral compositions relevant to scientific exploration and future resource utilization.

Ground – Surface and Terrain Characteristics. Provides information about ground conditions, supporting preliminary assessments of terrain accessibility and potential mobility limitations for astronauts and rovers.

Together, these layers allow users to evaluate multiple environmental and geological factors within a single interactive interface.

Level 2 – Detailed Mission Exploration (2D)

After selecting one of the three available rover missions, users can access a detailed two-dimensional map of the corresponding exploration region. The mission-level interface provides four additional overlays:

Resources - Displays locations of collected and analyzed samples, alongside selected areas with potential resource significance.

NASA Mission Route - Visualizes historical rover traversal routes, allowing users to examine previously explored terrain.

Coordinates - Provides a geographic coordinate grid to support spatial orientation and the identification of specific locations.

Astronaut Exploration Plan - Displays proposed exploration routes connecting selected scientific objectives and areas of potential resource interest.

By integrating these datasets, the platform provides a foundation for planning future surface exploration activities and evaluating potential destinations.

4. Astronaut Safety and Exploration Efficiency

Operating on the Martian surface presents significant challenges, including difficult terrain, extreme temperatures, limited resources, and environmental hazards. MAREK aims to support safer and more efficient exploration by providing astronauts with accessible information about their operating environment.

One of the platform's key capabilities is the visualization of terrain conditions that may influence route selection. Topographic data and ground characteristics help identify potentially hazardous areas, including steep slopes and terrain with limited traversability. The system also highlights regions exceeding a predefined 25-degree slope threshold, providing an additional indicator for preliminary terrain risk assessment. This threshold serves as a planning reference rather than a universal mobility limit, as safe traversal depends on vehicle capabilities, surface conditions, and mission requirements. By combining terrain analysis with historical rover routes and geological observations, the platform supports more informed exploration planning. 

Better preparation could help reduce unnecessary surface travel, limit astronauts' exposure to environmental hazards, and decrease the consumption of critical resources such as oxygen and energy. Ultimately, the project aims to support decision-making before and during future extravehicular activities (EVAs).

5. Supporting In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU)

A central objective of MAREK is to support the identification of local resources that could contribute to the development of Martian infrastructure. Transporting construction materials from Earth to Mars presents major logistical and economic challenges. ISRU offers an alternative approach by enabling future missions to investigate the extraction, processing, and utilization of resources already present on the Martian surface. MAREK supports this concept by integrating geological and geochemical observations that can help identify regions with potentially useful raw materials. The project initially focused on identifying areas containing raw materials required for geopolymer synthesis, which could potentially be used for road constructions, infrastructure components, and protection shield for Martian habitats.

The primary raw materials considered for geopolymer synthesis are sulfur and its derivatives, as well as Martian regolith.

Possible applications include:

  • Construction of roads and rover transportation routes.
  • Development of landing pads and other surface infrastructure.
  • Production of structural components for Martian bases.
  • Construction of protective barriers and shielding structures.

The platform does not directly perform resource extraction or material production. Instead, it provides geospatial information that could support the preliminary identification and evaluation of potential resource locations. By making scientific data more accessible for practical planning, the system could contribute to future efforts to reduce reliance on construction materials transported from Earth.

6. Future Development – Real-Time Navigation and HUD Integration

The current development phase focuses on geospatial visualization, scientific data integration, and exploration planning. Future development will expand the platform toward real-time astronaut navigation and enhanced situational awareness. One of the planned capabilities is integration with Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) technology. VIO combines visual information from cameras with measurements from inertial sensors to estimate movement and relative position. This approach is particularly relevant to Mars, where an Earth-like Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) is not currently available.

Because VIO estimates are subject to accumulated drift, reliable long-term positioning would require additional localization methods and reference information. Another planned development is integration with Head-Up Display (HUD) systems incorporated into astronaut helmets and Martian rovers. Such integration could allow navigation instructions, terrain information, and exploration objectives to be presented directly within the user's field of view.

Our long-term objective is to transform MAREK from a planning and visualization platform into a more comprehensive navigation support system for future surface operations.

7. Project Impact and Long-Term Vision

MAREK demonstrates how existing scientific datasets can be transformed into accessible tools supporting future human exploration. The project's value lies in combining several important aspects of Martian exploration within a single environment:

  • Scientific data integration: Bringing together orbital observations and rover measurements.
  • Exploration planning: Supporting the selection and evaluation of potential surface routes.
  • Astronaut safety: Providing terrain information relevant to preliminary risk assessment.
  • Resource identification: Supporting the search for materials potentially useful for Martian infrastructure.
  • Future navigation capabilities: Establishing a foundation for real-time positioning and augmented navigation interfaces.

Rather than treating geological analysis, route planning, and resource identification as separate activities, MAREK brings these functions together into one interactive platform. This integrated approach could improve the accessibility and practical value of NASA's publicly available scientific data.

Our long-term vision is to develop a comprehensive geospatial platform that supports scientific research, astronaut operations, and infrastructure planning for future human settlements on Mars.

MAREK aims to help turn scientific knowledge of the Martian surface into actionable information for safer exploration, more efficient resource utilization, and the sustainable expansion of humanity beyond Earth
